messages.content: I want to recover relightable geometry and materials from three images taken under unknown illumination. The goal also needs to quantify the ambiguity between shape, reflectance, and lighting. How should I understand those parts together?

The three images are the available visual evidence, but their illumination is unknown. The goal is to infer geometry and materials that can be used to predict appearance under relighting, while also representing the fact that the images may not uniquely determine shape, reflectance, and lighting. A shaded region, for example, might admit more than one explanation involving surface form, material response, or illumination. Quantifying ambiguity means not presenting one explanation as uniquely established when the images leave alternatives open.
So the aim is more than producing a plausible reconstruction of those three images?

Yes. A reconstruction that looks plausible in the three input images does not, by itself, establish that its geometry and materials will give good predictions under other lighting. “Relightable” makes those predictions central to the goal. The uncertainty aspect matters for the same reason: different explanations can look similar in the available images yet imply different appearances when relit.
Does unknown illumination mean we can treat differences in brightness as material differences?

Not automatically. When illumination is unknown, a brightness difference could be consistent with lighting, reflectance, shape, or some combination of them. The goal is to recover relightable geometry and materials while quantifying that ambiguity, rather than assigning every observed difference to one cause without qualification. The stated goal does not specify a particular way to separate the causes.
There are two numerical requirements. Can you state the relighting-quality one precisely?

Held-out relighting LPIPS should be reduced by 15% versus a matched point-estimate inverse renderer. LPIPS is the stated measure for that comparison, and lower is better. If the matched baseline’s held-out relighting LPIPS were denoted by B, a 15% reduction would correspond to 0.85B. That is a target, not a reported result.
Why specify a point-estimate inverse renderer as the comparison?

It makes the comparison explicit: the relighting LPIPS target is relative to a matched inverse renderer that produces a point estimate. The node does not say exactly how the renderers are matched, so it would be premature to supply matching criteria. Nor does that comparison alone say which explanation of shape, reflectance, or lighting is correct; it specifies the performance benchmark for held-out relighting.
And “held-out relighting” means the target is not just how well the three input images can be reproduced?

Right. The requirement names held-out relighting, rather than reconstruction of the three input images, as the setting in which LPIPS is evaluated. It does not give further details about the held-out conditions or evaluation procedure. The important distinction here is that fitting the available images and predicting relit appearance are not interchangeable claims.
What is the other numerical requirement asking for?

It asks for 85–95% coverage for nominal 90% predictive intervals on held-out relighting intensities. In general, coverage is the proportion of evaluated intensities that fall inside their associated predictive intervals. A nominal 90% interval carries a 90% coverage claim; the stated acceptable coverage range is 85–95%. As with the LPIPS threshold, this is a requirement to achieve, not an outcome already observed.
Is that interval about uncertainty in the geometry itself?

Not directly as worded. The specified coverage test concerns predictive intervals for held-out relighting intensities. Ambiguity in geometry, reflectance, and lighting can affect those predictions, but the stated 85–95% criterion is about where held-out intensities fall relative to the predicted intervals. It does not separately prescribe an interval-coverage test for recovered shapes or materials.
Would hitting the coverage range by itself satisfy the goal?

No. The goal includes recovering relightable geometry and materials and quantifying the shape–reflectance–lighting ambiguity. It also has both numerical requirements: a 15% reduction in held-out relighting LPIPS against the matched point-estimate inverse renderer, and 85–95% coverage for nominal 90% predictive intervals on held-out relighting intensities. Coverage addresses whether the predictive intervals contain intensities at the stated frequency; it does not replace the relighting-quality requirement.
Could LPIPS improve while the intervals still miss the coverage requirement?

Conceptually, yes. LPIPS evaluates the held-out relighting predictions under the specified comparison, while interval coverage evaluates how often held-out intensities lie within the predictive intervals. Better-looking relighting predictions do not, by themselves, establish that the intervals have appropriate coverage. Likewise, intervals with coverage in the required range do not establish the required LPIPS reduction.
When we say “quantify ambiguity,” should I read that as a claim that all three factors can be determined separately from these images?

No. It points to the possible trade-offs among shape, reflectance, and lighting when explaining the images. Quantifying ambiguity means acknowledging and expressing uncertainty in those explanations, rather than claiming the three images necessarily identify each factor uniquely. The node states the objective, not that unique recovery is possible or that any particular ambiguity has already been resolved.
Then the performance targets concern what the recovered representation predicts, while the ambiguity requirement concerns how confidently we attribute the images to shape, reflectance, and lighting?

That is a useful reading. The representation is meant to provide relightable geometry and materials, its held-out relighting is subject to the LPIPS comparison, and its predictive intervals for held-out relighting intensities are subject to the 85–95% coverage range. Alongside those tests, the goal asks that uncertainty between shape, reflectance, and unknown illumination be quantified rather than hidden behind a single confident explanation.
Could we use a three-image-conditioned normalizing flow over shape, BRDF, and illumination latents, then marginalize renderings to get relighting predictions and intervals?

That is the proposed approach. The flow would be trained to represent a distribution over shape, BRDF, and illumination latents conditioned on the three images. Rather than committing to one latent configuration, the proposal carries plausible configurations through rendering and marginalizes the resulting renderings into relighting predictions and predictive intervals.
What does “three-image-conditioned” add beyond saying we use three images?

It says the distribution over latents depends on the three images together. Those images provide the evidence used to infer plausible shape, reflectance, and illumination explanations. It does not say the illumination of the input images is known or supplied as a fixed input; illumination is among the latent quantities being inferred.
Why include illumination in the flow if the things we ultimately want are geometry and materials?

Because the images were formed under unknown illumination. An account of their appearance can trade off shape, BRDF, and lighting, so uncertainty about illumination is relevant to uncertainty about the recovered geometry and materials. Keeping illumination in the joint latent distribution lets those explanations remain linked rather than treating an assumed lighting estimate as certain.
Is BRDF just another name for the material in this proposal?

Here, the BRDF latents are the proposed representation of the material’s reflectance behavior. A BRDF concerns how a surface reflects light; it is distinct from both the surface’s shape and the illumination falling on it. The proposal does not specify a particular BRDF parameterization or a particular shape representation.
What work is the normalizing flow doing?

It is the proposed model for a conditional distribution over the joint latents, instead of a model that returns only a single estimate of each one. In general, a normalizing flow represents a flexible distribution through transformations of a simpler one. The point here is to retain multiple plausible shape–BRDF–illumination configurations when the three images do not settle on a unique explanation; the node does not prescribe the flow architecture.
Would it make sense to describe that as three separate uncertainty estimates?

Not quite. The proposal is a flow over shape, BRDF, and illumination latents jointly. The relationships among them matter: a change in one factor may be compatible with a change in another while still explaining the same images. Describing three unrelated uncertainty estimates would lose that aspect of the ambiguity the goal asks to quantify.
Can you make that distinction more concrete without assuming anything about the actual three images?

As a general illustration, one plausible interpretation of an image region might involve a different surface orientation, while another involves a different reflectance or illumination explanation. A joint distribution can represent which combinations remain plausible together. That illustration does not assert that any particular ambiguity occurs in the three images at hand.
Then what exactly does it mean to marginalize the renderings?

It means forming relighting predictions by accounting for renderings associated with the range of plausible latent configurations, rather than selecting one shape–BRDF–illumination configuration and using only its rendering. In probabilistic terms, the variability across relevant configurations is carried into the predicted appearance. The proposal does not fix a particular numerical integration or approximation method.
Is the interval over latent shapes, or over what the relit image will look like?

The intervals produced by marginalizing renderings are predictive intervals for relighting output. In the stated goal, the numerical coverage requirement specifically concerns held-out relighting intensities. The flow also represents uncertainty in shape, BRDF, and illumination latents, but an interval for a predicted intensity is not the same thing as an interval for geometry.
Does the unknown illumination of the three input images have to be the illumination used for every relighting prediction?

The proposal does not say that. Illumination latents address the unknown lighting involved in explaining the three conditioning images; relighting concerns predicted appearance under relighting conditions. The node does not specify how those conditions are supplied or how the renderings are constructed, so it would be too specific to impose a rule for that here.
Would marginalizing automatically give us nominal 90% intervals with the required coverage?

No. Marginalizing renderings supplies a way to derive a predictive distribution and intervals from uncertainty over the latents, but it does not guarantee calibration. The goal is 85–95% coverage for nominal 90% predictive intervals on held-out relighting intensities. Whether intervals from this proposal achieve that range would have to be assessed; it is not an established result.
And does the flow itself imply the LPIPS improvement?

No. The separate target is a 15% reduction in held-out relighting LPIPS versus a matched point-estimate inverse renderer. The flow-and-marginalization proposal is a way to make relighting predictions while retaining ambiguity; its use alone does not establish that LPIPS improvement. Nor does producing intervals substitute for meeting the LPIPS comparison.
So why not render only the most likely shape, BRDF, and lighting latents from the flow?

That would return to a single-configuration prediction and discard much of what the proposed distribution is meant to preserve. Marginalizing renderings allows different plausible configurations to contribute to predicted appearance and its uncertainty. This explains the intent of the proposal, not a claim that marginalization is guaranteed to outperform a point estimate.
Does the proposal tell us how the flow is trained or which renderings are included?

It says to train a three-image-conditioned normalizing flow over shape, BRDF, and illumination latents, and to marginalize renderings into relighting predictions and intervals. It does not specify a training objective, data source, latent parameterization, renderer, or marginalization procedure. Those details should not be read into the proposal as settled choices.
I think I see the division of labor: the flow retains plausible explanations of the three images, and rendering turns those explanations into predictions about relit appearance.

Yes. More precisely, the proposed flow models the joint uncertainty over shape, BRDF, and illumination given the three images; marginalizing renderings propagates that uncertainty into relighting predictions and intervals. That connects the shape–reflectance–lighting ambiguity to predictions that can be evaluated, without asserting that the ambiguity has already been resolved or that the numerical targets have been met.
How can inference from just three images preserve distinct geometry–BRDF–illumination explanations that produce similar observed pixels but different relightings?

The central distinction is between agreeing with the three observed images and agreeing about what would happen under relighting. Several joint settings of geometry, BRDF, and illumination might explain nearly the same observed pixels, yet make different relighting predictions. To preserve that ambiguity, inference needs to retain those settings as distinct plausible explanations rather than compressing them into one estimate merely because they fit the inputs similarly.
If their rendered input images look almost identical, what distinguishes the explanations during inference?

Their latent configurations can remain different even when their predictions for the observed pixels are similar. The question is whether the inference representation keeps track of those different configurations and their joint relationships. Similarity in the three input views is not, by itself, evidence that the configurations would behave identically under relighting.
Does the proposed three-image-conditioned flow do that automatically?

No. A flow over joint shape, BRDF, and illumination latents is a proposed way to represent a distribution rather than a single reconstruction. That gives a place for distinct explanations to be represented, but using a flow does not guarantee that inference will retain every relevant explanation or assign it appropriate weight. The question is partly about that gap between having a distributional model and actually preserving the ambiguity that matters for relighting.
Why emphasize a joint distribution instead of separate distributions for shape, BRDF, and illumination?

Because the explanations can depend on coordinated choices. A particular geometry might be plausible with one BRDF and illumination configuration, while a different geometry might be plausible with a different combination. Three independent summaries could suggest combinations that were never plausible together, or conceal the alternatives that were. A joint representation can, in principle, keep those dependencies intact.
Would taking the average of the plausible latents solve the problem more simply?

Not necessarily. An average latent setting need not correspond to any of the distinct plausible explanations, and a single averaged setting could obscure their different relighting behavior. Preserving ambiguity means keeping alternatives available through prediction, not assuming that one compromise configuration faithfully stands in for them all.
But if the observed pixels cannot distinguish two explanations, isn't choosing one unavoidable?

Choosing one is an option for a point estimate, but it is not logically required of an uncertainty-aware inference. The three images may leave the explanations unresolved, in which case the honest output can retain uncertainty between them. That does not claim the images contain enough information to identify the correct explanation; it avoids turning a lack of distinction in the inputs into unwarranted certainty.
What role does illumination play in keeping those alternatives separate?

Because the illumination of the input images is unknown, it is part of each explanation of their pixels. If illumination is fixed to one assumed value without accounting for uncertainty, some shape–BRDF alternatives might be ruled out or favored for that assumption alone. Keeping illumination alongside shape and BRDF allows the inference to represent alternative combinations that explain the observations. It does not mean that every combination is equally plausible.
Could two explanations be effectively interchangeable for the three inputs but not interchangeable for the relighting predictions?

Yes—that is the precise difficulty raised by the question. Their agreement on the observed pixels only establishes agreement under those observed conditions. Relighting asks how the inferred geometry and reflectance would respond in another lighting situation, where the explanations may diverge. Treating input-image agreement as proof of predictive equivalence would erase the ambiguity the goal asks to quantify.
How would marginalizing renderings help rather than hide that divergence?

If the distinct plausible configurations are retained, their renderings can contribute to a distribution of relighting outcomes. That distribution can reflect disagreement instead of returning only the rendering of a selected configuration. Marginalization helps propagate the ambiguity into predictions and intervals; it cannot recover alternatives that inference has already discarded.
Could a single relighting prediction still conceal the fact that there are several very different possible outcomes?

It could. A single summary of a predictive distribution may not reveal whether its variability comes from nearby outcomes or from separated alternatives. The broader predictive distribution is what carries that distinction. Likewise, an interval for an intensity communicates a range and can be evaluated for coverage, but one interval alone need not display the structure of all the explanations behind it.
Then is the challenge to preserve distinct explanations in latent space, or distinct outcomes in relighting space?

Both matter, but they are not identical. Distinct geometry–BRDF–illumination configurations may produce similar observed pixels; preserving them in the joint latent distribution keeps their interpretations separate. Carrying them through rendering reveals whether—and how—they differ in relighting space. If they predict the same relighting outcome, their latent distinction may not affect that particular prediction; if they differ, collapsing them would conceal predictive ambiguity.
Does this question imply that the three images definitely contain two or more such explanations?

No. It asks how inference can preserve distinct explanations when they yield similar observed pixels but different relightings. It does not report that a particular set of three images has a known number of explanations, or that any specific geometry, BRDF, or illumination alternative has been found.
Can the nominal 90% predictive intervals tell us whether those explanations were preserved?

Coverage of nominal 90% intervals on held-out relighting intensities is relevant to whether predictive uncertainty is calibrated at that level; the goal specifies 85–95% coverage. But coverage alone would not identify which latent explanations were retained or show their structure. Conversely, displaying several latent explanations would not by itself establish the required coverage. They speak to related but different aspects of the question.
And how does the held-out relighting LPIPS target relate to this ambiguity?

It tests relighting quality under the stated comparison: a 15% reduction in held-out relighting LPIPS versus a matched point-estimate inverse renderer is the target. Preserving plausible explanations could be useful for predictions, but neither their presence nor the proposed flow guarantees that improvement. The question here is specifically how not to lose alternatives whose input pixels look alike even though their relightings differ.
So an inference result that fits all three images closely could still fail to answer this question?

Yes. Close agreement with the three images does not show whether alternative explanations survived inference, especially when those alternatives agree on the observed pixels. Answering the question requires attention to whether joint shape–BRDF–illumination ambiguity is retained and passed through to relighting predictions, rather than judged only by fit to the inputs.
Would it be accurate to say the proposed flow provides the representation, while this question asks whether the representation actually keeps the relighting-relevant distinctions?

That is accurate. The proposal names a three-image-conditioned normalizing flow over shape, BRDF, and illumination latents and marginalization of renderings. This question probes a crucial property that proposal would need: retaining distinct, jointly plausible explanations despite their similar observed pixels, so that differences in their relightings are not silently lost. It remains an open question here, not a demonstrated capability.

Here is the hypothesis I want to examine: a likelihood-trained flow with lighting augmentation retains competing shape–BRDF–light modes, achieves at least 15% lower LPIPS than point estimates, and gives 85–95% interval coverage. Is that a fair statement?

Yes, as a hypothesis rather than a result. It proposes that likelihood training together with lighting augmentation will help the flow preserve competing joint explanations of the three images, and that the resulting relighting predictions will meet both quantitative targets. The ≥15% LPIPS improvement and 85–95% coverage have not been established by stating the hypothesis.
What are “competing shape–BRDF–light modes” in this context?

They are distinct plausible regions of the joint latent distribution: one combination of shape, BRDF, and illumination could explain the observed pixels, while another combination could explain them similarly. Calling them competing modes emphasizes that the alternatives should remain distinguishable rather than being reduced to one shape, one reflectance, and one lighting estimate. Their significance for this question is that they may predict different appearances under relighting.
Does the hypothesis say that the three images uniquely determine which mode is right?

No. It says the flow retains competing modes. That is an uncertainty claim, not a claim of unique identification. The possibility that different explanations fit similar observed pixels is exactly why retaining alternatives matters.
What does “likelihood-trained” contribute to the statement?

It identifies likelihood training as part of the hypothesized approach to learning the flow’s distribution, rather than training it solely to return one preferred latent configuration. The hypothesis is that this contributes to retaining competing explanations. It does not specify the likelihood formulation or prove that likelihood training will, in practice, preserve every relighting-relevant mode.
And why mention lighting augmentation specifically?

The hypothesized role is to help the model avoid treating one lighting explanation as the only plausible account of the three images. Since lighting can trade off with shape and BRDF in explaining pixels, variation involving lighting could be relevant to retaining those joint alternatives. That is the rationale within the hypothesis, not an observed effect, and the statement does not specify how the augmentation is performed.
Does lighting augmentation mean we suddenly know the illumination in the three input images?

No. The inference problem still concerns three images under unknown illumination. Mentioning lighting augmentation in training does not turn the input illumination into a known quantity or change the number of input images. The hypothesis gives no further details about the augmentation.
Could I interpret the hypothesis as keeping separate shape modes, separate BRDF modes, and separate light modes?

That wording might miss the important joint structure. The competing modes are shape–BRDF–light explanations: particular choices can remain plausible in combination even if swapping one component independently would not. The hypothesis is about retaining those competing combinations, not merely broadening three unrelated distributions.
If the flow has several modes, has it necessarily retained the modes that matter for relighting?

No. A multimodal distribution could still omit a plausible explanation or assign it too little weight. The hypothesis specifically concerns competing explanations that fit similar observed pixels but may yield different relightings. Whether the trained flow retains those relevant alternatives is part of what remains to be established.
How does that connect to the LPIPS part of the hypothesis?

The proposed connection is that retaining and propagating those alternatives could improve relighting predictions compared with point estimates. The quantitative claim is at least 15% lower LPIPS versus point estimates; in the stated goal, this is a held-out relighting comparison against a matched point-estimate inverse renderer. Preserving modes is a proposed reason the approach might help, not proof that the LPIPS threshold will be reached.
When you say “at least 15% lower,” what exactly is the comparison?

It is a relative reduction in LPIPS, not a subtraction of 15 LPIPS units. For a comparison value B, at least 15% lower means no more than 0.85B. The relevant goal measures LPIPS on held-out relighting and compares against a matched point-estimate inverse renderer. The hypothesis supplies a predicted outcome for that comparison, not a measured value.
Does the 85–95% range mean we are trying to make intervals that contain 85–95% of every individual relighting?

No. Coverage refers to the proportion of evaluated held-out relighting intensities that fall within their predictive intervals. The goal specifies nominal 90% predictive intervals and asks for observed coverage of 85–95%. It is an aggregate coverage requirement, not a guarantee about each individual intensity.
Would an interval count as successful just because it is very wide?

Not automatically. The stated numerical criterion is 85–95% coverage for nominal 90% predictive intervals; intervals that contain far more than 95% of the evaluated intensities would be outside that range. Coverage is also only one requirement: the hypothesis separately predicts at least 15% lower held-out relighting LPIPS versus point estimates. The node does not set an additional numerical interval-width target.
Could the flow retain competing modes but still miss the coverage range?

Yes. Retaining distinct latent explanations does not ensure their predictive probabilities are appropriately weighted, or that the resulting intervals have the desired empirical coverage. Mode retention and 85–95% coverage are related parts of the hypothesis, but one does not establish the other.
Could it reach the LPIPS target while failing to retain those competing explanations?

That is conceptually possible: an LPIPS comparison measures relighting prediction quality, not whether distinct shape–BRDF–light interpretations remain represented. The hypothesis makes both claims, so a favorable LPIPS value alone would not establish its mode-retention claim. Conversely, evidence of retained modes alone would not establish the quantitative LPIPS or coverage claims.
Is the hypothesis that likelihood training and lighting augmentation each independently achieve the targets?

No. It names a likelihood-trained flow with lighting augmentation as the proposed combination. It does not assign separate effects to likelihood training and augmentation, or claim that either one alone would achieve the LPIPS and coverage targets.
What should I avoid claiming before this hypothesis is tested?

Avoid saying that the flow already preserves the competing modes, that it has already reduced held-out relighting LPIPS by ≥15% versus point estimates, or that its nominal 90% intervals already have 85–95% coverage. Those are the outcomes the hypothesis anticipates. It also does not specify enough implementation detail to claim a particular flow design, augmentation procedure, or likelihood formulation.
So the idea is not merely “use uncertainty,” but that this particular training combination might keep explanations separate and translate that into better relighting and calibrated intervals?

Exactly. The hypothesis links a likelihood-trained flow with lighting augmentation to preservation of competing joint shape–BRDF–light modes, then predicts two outcomes: ≥15% lower held-out relighting LPIPS relative to point estimates and 85–95% coverage for the nominal 90% intervals on held-out relighting intensities. Each link remains a hypothesis, including the claim that preserving those alternatives will translate into those measured outcomes.

For the evaluation activity, compare augmented and unaugmented flows with matched point estimates on TriLight-Synth, using held-out relighting LPIPS and 90% intensity-interval coverage. What does that comparison cover?

It names TriLight-Synth as the evaluation setting, three kinds of estimates to compare—augmented flows, unaugmented flows, and matched point estimates—and two measurements: LPIPS on held-out relighting and coverage of 90% intensity intervals. It describes an evaluation to carry out, not results from one.
Is “augmented” referring to the lighting augmentation in the hypothesis?

Yes. In this context, the augmented-versus-unaugmented flow comparison concerns lighting augmentation. The activity does not specify what that augmentation consists of, so it would be premature to describe particular lighting changes or training examples.
Why include an unaugmented flow as well as point estimates?

They provide different comparisons. Comparing augmented and unaugmented flows lets the evaluation examine differences associated with using lighting augmentation within the flow approach. Comparing the flows with matched point estimates places their relighting LPIPS alongside a point-estimate alternative. Those comparisons do not, by themselves, establish why any difference occurs.
Does “matched point estimates” tell us exactly what has been matched?

No. It says the point estimates should be matched for the comparison, but the activity does not define the matching criteria. We can preserve that requirement without assuming particular training conditions, representations, or other controls that have not been specified.
Which measurement tells us whether the relit images are better?

Held-out relighting LPIPS is the named measure for comparing relighting predictions. Lower LPIPS indicates better performance under that measure. The activity does not provide any LPIPS values or say which of the compared approaches performs best.
And what is counted for 90% intensity-interval coverage?

For each evaluated intensity with a nominal 90% predictive interval, coverage asks whether the held-out intensity falls inside that interval. The coverage figure is the proportion that do. It assesses the intervals’ predictive coverage, not the similarity of a single relit image under LPIPS.
Should we expect a point estimate to have 90% intervals too?

Not from this activity as stated. Point estimates are part of the comparison, particularly for relighting LPIPS. The activity names intensity-interval coverage as a measurement but does not say that the matched point-estimate method supplies predictive intervals. We should not invent such an output for it.
So can the LPIPS and coverage figures be read as interchangeable scores?

No. LPIPS evaluates held-out relighting predictions under a perceptual similarity measure. Coverage evaluates how often held-out intensities fall within nominal 90% predictive intervals. A method could have a favorable value on one measure without that telling us its value on the other; the activity calls for considering both.
If the augmented flow has different coverage from the unaugmented one, would that prove it retained more competing shape–BRDF–light explanations?

No. A coverage difference would describe the behavior of their predictive intervals on the evaluated intensities. It would not, on its own, reveal which joint shape–BRDF–light explanations either flow retained. The comparison is relevant to the hypothesis, but the two stated measurements do not directly display the structure of the latent distribution.
Would similar LPIPS values mean the two flows represent the same ambiguity?

Not necessarily. Similar held-out relighting LPIPS values could coexist with different predictive intervals or different distributions over shape, BRDF, and illumination. LPIPS is useful for the stated relighting comparison, but it is not a complete description of what either flow represents.
What if both flows cover more than 90% of the intensities? Is that automatically preferable?

Not automatically. Coverage needs to be interpreted against the nominal 90% level; simply increasing the fraction inside the intervals is not an unqualified improvement. The activity asks to measure coverage, but supplies neither results nor interval widths. We cannot infer from the activity that either flow is appropriately calibrated.
Does this activity say how the held-out relightings are selected on TriLight-Synth?

No. It specifies held-out relighting LPIPS as an evaluation measure on TriLight-Synth, without giving a selection procedure or other details of the held-out evaluation. Those should remain unspecified rather than being filled in with an assumed protocol.
Can I say the comparison has already shown that lighting augmentation improves relighting?

No. The activity says to compare augmented and unaugmented flows with matched point estimates; it reports no comparison outcomes. An improvement, a lack of improvement, or a difference in interval coverage would all require results that have not been supplied here.
Then the clean description is that TriLight-Synth is where we make the comparison, LPIPS measures held-out relighting, and coverage checks the nominal 90% intensity intervals?

Yes. Keep the compared approaches explicit—augmented flows, unaugmented flows, and matched point estimates—and keep the two measurements distinct. That fully describes the stated evaluation activity without implying that it has been run or that any of the approaches has met a performance target.
What did the TriLight-Synth comparison find for the augmented flow?

The augmented flow’s held-out relighting LPIPS was 0.142, compared with 0.171 for the point estimate—a reported 17% reduction. Its nominal 90% intensity intervals covered 91% of the evaluated intensities, compared with 76% coverage for the unaugmented flow.
Are the LPIPS and coverage figures comparing the augmented flow against the same alternative?

No. The LPIPS comparison given here is augmented flow versus point estimate: 0.142 versus 0.171. The interval-coverage comparison is augmented flow versus unaugmented flow: 91% versus 76%. The evidence does not give an LPIPS value for the unaugmented flow or an interval-coverage value for the point estimate.
Can you check how the 17% LPIPS reduction is calculated?
The difference is 0.171 − 0.142 = 0.029. Dividing by the point-estimate value, 0.029 ÷ 0.171, gives about 0.170, or 17%. It is a relative reduction from 0.171, not a decrease of 17 LPIPS units.
And the coverage difference is 15%, right?

It is a difference of 15 percentage points: 91% minus 76%. Calling it a 15% relative increase would mean something different. Both figures describe coverage of nominal 90% intensity intervals, with 91% reported for the augmented flow and 76% for the unaugmented flow.
How should I interpret 91% coverage for a nominal 90% interval?

It means that 91% of the evaluated held-out relighting intensities fell inside intervals designated to have 90% predictive coverage. Nominal coverage and observed coverage are distinct: 90% describes the intervals’ stated level, while 91% is the observed proportion on TriLight-Synth.
Does 76% coverage mean the unaugmented flow’s intervals were narrower?

The figures alone do not establish their widths. They show that the unaugmented flow’s nominal 90% intervals contained 76% of the evaluated intensities, substantially fewer than the augmented flow’s 91%. Interval widths or the reason for the difference are not reported in this evidence.
Do these numbers show that the augmented flow retained distinct shape–BRDF–light modes?

They show the stated relighting LPIPS and intensity-interval coverage outcomes on TriLight-Synth. They do not directly show the flow’s latent modes or identify particular competing shape–BRDF–light explanations. The coverage contrast is relevant to the proposed uncertainty-aware approach, but it should not be presented as a direct observation of mode retention.
Could I infer the unaugmented flow’s relighting LPIPS from its 76% coverage?
No. LPIPS and interval coverage measure different properties, and no unaugmented-flow LPIPS value is supplied. Its 76% coverage cannot be converted into a relighting LPIPS score.
What is the most precise short statement of the evidence, without adding outcomes we have not measured?

On TriLight-Synth, the augmented flow recorded held-out relighting LPIPS of 0.142 versus 0.171 for the point estimate, or 17% lower. Its nominal 90% intensity intervals had 91% coverage, versus 76% for the unaugmented flow. Those are the reported comparisons; they do not supply the other methods’ values on the respective measures or directly characterize the retained latent explanations.
What is the decision following the TriLight-Synth evaluation?

Advance the lighting-augmented flow to real-image validation. The decision rests on TriLight-Synth meeting both the held-out relighting LPIPS reduction target and the predictive-coverage target. It is a decision to validate on real images, not a claim that real-image validation has already succeeded.
What does “both targets” refer to here?

The relighting target is at least a 15% reduction in held-out LPIPS against a matched point-estimate inverse renderer. The uncertainty target is 85–95% coverage for nominal 90% predictive intervals on held-out relighting intensities. The decision states that the lighting-augmented flow meets both on TriLight-Synth.
Does that mean the ambiguity between shape, BRDF, and lighting has been resolved?

No. Meeting the relighting and coverage targets does not mean the three images uniquely determine shape, reflectance, and illumination. Nor does this decision independently establish which competing latent explanations the flow retains. It says the specified predictive targets have been met on TriLight-Synth and advances the approach for validation with real images.
Why say “advance to real-image validation” rather than “use it on real images”?

Because those make different claims. Advancing to validation means the lighting-augmented flow is the approach to examine next in a real-image setting. Saying it is already validated or ready for general real-image use would go beyond this decision. The TriLight-Synth outcome establishes the stated targets in that evaluation setting, not in every setting.
Is there a real-image performance target or validation protocol in the decision?

No. The decision names real-image validation as the next stage, but it does not specify a dataset, protocol, schedule, or numerical real-image result. Those details should not be inferred from the fact that the flow is being advanced.
Are we also advancing the unaugmented flow and the point-estimate renderer?

The decision specifically names the lighting-augmented flow for real-image validation. The other approaches provided comparisons in the TriLight-Synth evaluation; this decision does not say they are being advanced, nor does it make a broader decision about their use.
